title: What Is Subject To Financing in Real Estate? A Complete Investor's Guide
excerpt: Subject to financing lets investors take over a seller's existing mortgage without qualifying for a new loan. Learn how this creative strategy works, when to use it, and how to protect yourself.

sections.content: If you have ever heard an investor say they bought a house without getting a new loan, there is a good chance they used subject to financing. This creative strategy lets you take over a seller's existing mortgage and make payments on it — without the bank ever knowing ownership has changed. It sounds unusual, but it is completely legal and has helped thousands of investors close deals quickly with little money down. Whether you are just starting out or looking to expand your portfolio, understanding subject to financing can open doors that traditional lending keeps shut. For a broader look at all your options, check out the [How to Finance Real Estate Investments: Complete Guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-investing-financing).
What Is Subject To Financing in Real Estate?

Subject to financing — often called 'sub-to' — means you purchase a property subject to the existing mortgage staying in place. The deed transfers to you, the new owner, but the original loan remains in the seller's name with their lender. You simply take over the monthly payments. The phrase 'subject to' refers to the fact that the sale is made subject to the existing financing continuing as-is.

Here is a simple example. A homeowner owes $140,000 on a 30-year mortgage at a 3.5% interest rate. They have fallen behind on payments and need to sell fast. Their home is worth $185,000. You agree to take over their $140,000 loan, bring it current if needed, and give them perhaps $5,000 in cash to walk away. You now control a $185,000 asset with roughly $45,000 in built-in equity — without ever applying for a loan. Your monthly payment stays at whatever the seller was paying, which in this case could be around $628 per month on principal and interest.
How Does a Subject To Deal Actually Work?
Step-by-Step Process

items: Find a motivated seller — ideally someone facing foreclosure, divorce, job loss, or a pressing need to relocate quickly
Verify the existing loan terms: remaining balance, interest rate, monthly payment, and whether it is current or in default
Negotiate the purchase price and any cash the seller will receive at closing
Work with a real estate attorney to draft a subject to agreement and transfer the deed
Set up payment directly to the lender or through a third-party servicing company to protect both parties
Record the deed at the county courthouse to officially establish ownership
Begin making payments on the original mortgage and manage the property as you see fit

sections.content: Always use a reputable title company and real estate attorney when closing a subject to deal. Cutting corners on paperwork can expose you to serious legal and financial risk. Budget $500–$1,500 for proper closing costs — it is worth every penny.
Why Sellers Agree to Subject To Deals

You might wonder why any seller would hand over their home while leaving their name on the mortgage. The answer comes down to desperation and convenience. Sellers in distress — facing foreclosure, a job transfer, medical debt, or a nasty divorce — often care more about getting out fast than maximizing their sales price. A subject to deal gives them an immediate exit. Their credit gets protected if they were behind on payments, and they walk away without the cloud of foreclosure following them for seven years.
The best subject to deals happen when you solve a real problem for someone. You are not taking advantage of a seller — you are offering them a lifeline when traditional options have run out.
The Due-on-Sale Clause: The Biggest Risk You Need to Know

Almost every conventional mortgage includes a due-on-sale clause. This clause allows the lender to demand full repayment of the loan if the property changes ownership without their approval. In theory, the bank could call the note due the moment they discover you have taken the property subject to. In practice, lenders rarely do this — especially when payments are being made on time. Banks are in the business of collecting payments, not foreclosing on performing loans. However, the risk is real and you must understand it before proceeding.

Experienced investors manage this risk by keeping payments on time, maintaining insurance in both names, and having a clear exit strategy — whether that is a refinance, a flip, or an assignment to another buyer. If you want to compare this risk against other non-traditional funding methods, read our breakdown of [Hard Money Loans Explained: How They Work for Investors](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/hard-money-loans-explained) for context on what lenders actually care about.
Subject To vs. Other Creative Financing Strategies

Subject to is just one tool in a creative investor's toolkit. It works best when the seller has a low-interest mortgage you want to preserve — locking in a 3% or 4% rate when current rates are near 7% is a massive financial advantage. But it is not always the right fit. Sometimes a [HELOC for real estate investing](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/heloc-real-estate-investing) makes more sense if you already own equity in another property. Other times, using [private money lenders](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/private-money-lenders-guide) gives you more flexibility and cleaner title. The key is matching the right financing tool to the right deal.
When Subject To Makes the Most Sense

items: The existing mortgage has a low interest rate (below current market rates)
The seller is in distress and needs a fast close with no realtor commissions
You have limited cash or cannot qualify for traditional financing right now
The remaining loan balance is well below current market value
You plan to hold the property as a rental and want low monthly payments
The property is in a high-demand market where appreciation is likely

sections.content: How to Analyze a Subject To Deal

Numbers matter more than the excitement of a creative deal structure. Before agreeing to any subject to purchase, run the full math. What is the monthly payment you are inheriting? What will the property rent for? What are taxes, insurance, and maintenance costs? Is there deferred maintenance you need to budget for? Use the free [Mortgage Calculator at aiwholesail.com/tools/mortgage-calculator](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/mortgage-calculator) to model different scenarios and make sure the deal cash flows positively before you commit.

Always order a title search before closing any subject to deal. You need to know if there are second liens, back taxes, HOA judgments, or other encumbrances attached to the property. Inheriting hidden debt can turn a great deal into a nightmare.
Where to Find Subject To Deals

Subject to deals are not listed on the MLS. They come from motivated sellers, and finding them requires consistent outreach. Pre-foreclosure lists, driving for dollars, direct mail campaigns, and bandit signs are all proven sources. Hot markets like [Dallas, TX](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx), [Atlanta, GA](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga), and [Charlotte, NC](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/charlotte-nc) have high concentrations of distressed sellers and active investor communities where subject to deals regularly surface. Building relationships with foreclosure attorneys, probate attorneys, and real estate agents who specialize in distressed properties can also put you in front of sellers before anyone else.

If you are new to finding off-market opportunities, our [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) walks through exactly how to locate and approach motivated sellers. And if you are just getting started in real estate investing overall, the [Real Estate Investing for Beginners guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-investing-for-beginners) gives you the full foundation before you dive into advanced strategies like subject to.
Protecting Yourself as the Buyer

items: Use a land trust to hold the property — this adds a layer of privacy and can reduce due-on-sale triggers
Get title insurance to protect against undisclosed liens or ownership disputes
Set up a third-party loan servicer to handle payments and maintain a professional paper trail
Keep the seller's insurance active and add yourself as an additional insured party
Document everything in writing and have your attorney review all agreements before signing
Have a refinance plan ready so you can move the loan into your name within 12–24 months if needed
